_meta.description: Mapping of finding types to Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) outcomes. CAF is the UK National Cyber Security Centre's outcomes-based framework used by regulators. Objective B (Protecting Against Cyber Attack) is where most cloud misconfigurations land.
_meta.mapping_rationale: CAF is outcomes-based, not control-based. Each outcome describes a state the organisation should reach; mappings link finding types to the outcome(s) they most directly compromise. Most cloud misconfigurations land in Objective B (Protecting Against Cyber Attack), since that is where technical misconfigurations sit. Detection-oriented findings are mapped to Objective C (Detecting Cyber Security Events) instead, on the same 'most direct outcome' logic, rather than being forced into B for consistency.

audit_notes.S3_PUBLIC_VIA_ACL: Two references. B2.a is primary — a bucket readable by AllUsers has bypassed identity verification and authorisation entirely. B3.a is secondary and softer — 'Understanding Data' captures the case where the organisation may not know that the misconfigured bucket contains sensitive data. B3.a is defensible but weaker than B2.a.
audit_notes.S3_PUBLIC_ACCESS_BLOCK_DISABLED: B4.a covers 'Secure by design'. PAB is the security-by-default configuration for S3 buckets; leaving it disabled is a design failure. This mapping is clean.
audit_notes.S3_ENCRYPTION_DISABLED: B3.c covers 'Stored data' outcomes and explicitly includes encryption at rest as a control. This mapping is unambiguous.
audit_notes.S3_VERSIONING_DISABLED: B5.a covers Resilience Preparation — ensuring the organisation is resilient to and can recover from a cyber attack or operational failure. Versioning is a recovery mechanism at the object level; disabling it removes a specific, low-cost resilience control this outcome expects to be in place.
audit_notes.S3_LOGGING_DISABLED: First finding mapped outside Objective B. C1.a (Monitoring Coverage, under Objective C: Detecting Cyber Security Events) is the honest fit — access logging is a detection capability, not a protection one, and CAF's own structure separates the two. Forcing this into an Objective B outcome would have been the more consistent-looking choice but the less accurate one.
audit_notes.S3_LIFECYCLE_MISSING: B3.a covers 'Understanding data', already used as a secondary reference for S3_PUBLIC_VIA_ACL. A lifecycle policy is fundamentally a statement of what data exists and how long it should be kept — the same outcome CAF is describing. Reused here as the primary reference rather than introduced as a new outcome.
audit_notes.S3_TLS_NOT_ENFORCED: B3.b covers 'Data in transit protection', a distinct B3 sub-outcome from B3.c (Stored data, used for encryption at rest). CAF separates the two explicitly, so this mapping does too rather than collapsing them the way NIS2's single cryptography clause does.
audit_notes.KMS_KEY_ROTATION_DISABLED: B3.c, reused from S3_ENCRYPTION_DISABLED. Key rotation is a control on the mechanism that protects stored data, not the data itself, but the outcome it serves is the same one B3.c describes.
audit_notes.KMS_KEY_PENDING_DELETION: B5.a reused from S3_VERSIONING_DISABLED, not B3.c — this finding is about losing a recovery capability, not about a stored-data control weakening. Same Resilience Preparation outcome as the versioning finding, for the same reason.
audit_notes.IAM_ROOT_ACCESS_KEYS_ACTIVE: B2.a reused from S3_PUBLIC_VIA_ACL's primary reference. Active root keys are an identity/authentication control gap at the account level rather than the bucket level, but the same CAF outcome — unrestricted, unverified access — applies.
